sections.title: Hungarian dishes explained
paragraphs: Gulyás is the dish visitors most often get wrong. In Hungary it is a soup, even though English-language menus often call it a stew. It is described as a one-pot dish seasoned with paprika, usually built on beef or mutton with onion, caraway, potatoes, carrots and small pinched noodles called csipetke. The word means cattle herder, which points to its origin on the plains. Pörkölt is its thicker cousin: a stew of meat, onion and sweet paprika that can be made with chicken, pork or other meat, and paprikás is the version finished with sour cream. If you want the soup, ask for gulyásleves; if you want a stew on rice or with dumplings, look for pörkölt or paprikás.

Lángos is fried yeast dough, traditionally eaten warm, with toppings such as sour cream, grated cheese, sausage, bacon or garlic. It began as a way of using leftover bread dough and is sold at markets, fairs and fast-food counters. Kürtőskalács, the chimney cake, is a strip of sweet yeast dough wound around a spit, rolled in sugar and roasted over charcoal until the sugar forms a crisp caramel crust; it is associated with the Székely people of Transylvania, and the first written record dates from 1679. Dobos torte, a sponge cake layered with chocolate buttercream under a hard caramel top, was introduced by the Budapest delicatessen owner József C. Dobos at the 1885 national exhibition.

Two more names to know are túrós csusza, egg noodles with túró (a fresh curd cheese, similar to quark), served savoury with bacon or sweet with sugar, and halászlé, a hot paprika fish soup whose recipe varies between the Danube and Tisza river regions. Rétes, the strudel, is the traditional pastry. Menus and recipes differ from place to place, so treat these descriptions as a guide to what to expect, not a rulebook.
bullets: Gulyás is a soup; pörkölt is a thicker stew; paprikás adds sour cream.
Lángos and kürtőskalács are snacks to share while walking.
Ask staff how a dish is prepared if you have a food allergy.

sections.title: How a Hungarian meal works, and what to drink
paragraphs: Traditionally, lunch is the main meal of the day and may have several courses: soup first, then a main dish, then dessert. Dinner is described as less important, and there is no single typical Hungarian dinner. Traditional cooking rests on meat, seasonal vegetables, fruit, bread and dairy, with chicken, pork and beef the everyday meats. Paprika is the defining spice, and both sweet and hot varieties are common, so a Hungarian menu is not automatically fiery.

Hungary has several wine regions. Tokaj in the north-east is the best known, famous for the sweet Tokaji aszú, made from individually picked grapes affected by noble rot, and also for dry Furmint; the Tokaj wine region was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape in 2002. Eger is associated with the red blend Egri Bikavér, and Etyek-Buda, close to Budapest, is known for fresh white wines. Ask a wine bar or restaurant for a glass of a region you have not tried.

Pálinka is a fruit brandy, usually from plums, apricots, apples, pears or cherries. Under Hungary's 2008 law only a spirit made from Hungarian-grown fruit and distilled and bottled in Hungary may carry the name, and it has had EU protected status since 2004. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur made by the Zwack company from a secret blend of herbs and aged in oak casks; it is usually taken as a digestif and is described as an acquired taste. Drink both slowly: they are strong spirits, not table wines.

sections.title: The Great Market Hall and other markets
paragraphs: The Great Market Hall at Fővám tér is Budapest's largest and oldest indoor market. It was designed by Samu Pecz and opened on 15 February 1897, and its roof is covered in coloured Zsolnay tiles. Inside, the ground floor is mostly produce, meat, pastries, spices and spirits, an upper level holds food stalls and souvenirs, and the basement has fish and pickled vegetables. The hall was badly damaged in the Second World War, and a renovation begun in 1991 led to its reopening in 1997. Walk the whole hall before you buy: prices and quality differ from stall to stall.

Other markets give a more local picture. The Rákóczi tér Market Hall in District VIII was one of the big halls of the 1890s. It was destroyed by fire in 1988 and rebuilt, reopening in 1991; it is a working neighbourhood market, mostly meat and groceries. The Lehel Market Hall in District XIII at Váci út, designed to look like a ship, is described by local-food writers as a neighbourhood hall for fresh produce, cheese, sausages and lángos. The Fény utca market, on the Buda side near Széll Kálmán tér, is described as a semi-open-air, multi-storey market with produce, baked goods, wine and seasonal events.

Sources disagree on details such as the opening year of the Rákóczi tér hall, which is given as 1894 in some places (when building began) and 1897 elsewhere, and on traders and hours, which change. Check each market's current arrangements before a special trip, and note that market halls are working shops first and sightseeing stops second.

sections.title: Coffee houses and pastry, with their history
paragraphs: Café Gerbeaud on Vörösmarty tér has a long story. Henrik Kugler founded the business in 1858 and moved it to what is now Vörösmarty tér in 1870. He invited the confectioner Émile Gerbeaud to Budapest in 1884, and Gerbeaud eventually took over the business and kept the name. Today its own website highlights its pastry selection, its coffee blend and classic sweets such as cognac sour cherries and cat's tongues.

The New York Café on Erzsébet körút opened on 23 October 1894 on the ground floor of a New York insurance company building, and was long a meeting place for Hungarian writers and poets. After the Second World War the café was renamed Hungaria in 1954 and regained its original name in 1989. The building was later restored and reopened as a hotel with the café inside. Because it is both a historic interior and a popular stop, allow extra time and read the venue's own page for seating and reservation rules.

A practical approach: choose one historic café for atmosphere and eat the rest of your pastry at neighbourhood confectioners, where the focus is on the cake itself. Order a Dobos torte, a rétes or a slice of whatever the display case recommends, and let the coffee house be a rest from sightseeing rather than a race through the sights.

sections.title: Special diets and food experiences
paragraphs: Traditional Hungarian cuisine is built on meat, so vegetarians may find the classic menu limited, and traditional sweets often contain a lot of egg and dairy. Dedicated vegetarian, vegan, gluten-free and kosher kitchens exist in Budapest, especially in the central districts and in Erzsébetváros, the old Jewish Quarter, where a glatt kosher Hungarian-Jewish restaurant is listed by one city directory. On menus, look for the words vegán, gluténmentes and kóser. Listings of such places are compiled by third parties and details differ, so confirm certification, kitchen practice and halal or kosher status directly with the venue.

If you would like help with orientation, food experiences come in several types. Guided culinary and wine walks, sommelier-led wine tastings and visits to food markets are all offered by local companies, and some multi-day programmes include baking Hungarian holiday desserts. Read what each experience actually covers before choosing, and remember that none of these is needed: a market stroll and a coffee-house stop already give you a fair taste of the city.

faqs.question: Is gulyás in Budapest a soup or a stew?
faqs.answer: In Hungary gulyás is a paprika-flavoured soup, usually made with beef, onion, potatoes and small noodles. The thicker dish that English speakers often call goulash is closer to pörkölt, so check the menu wording if you want a stew.

faqs.question: What are Hungarian pálinka and Unicum?
faqs.answer: Pálinka is a Hungarian fruit brandy, often from plums, apricots or pears, and the name is legally protected. Unicum is a bitter herbal liqueur made by the Zwack company and usually drunk as a digestif. Both are strong, so sip slowly.

faqs.question: Is Budapest food hard for vegetarians?
faqs.answer: Traditional Hungarian cooking is meat-heavy, so classic menus can be limited for vegetarians. Dedicated vegetarian and vegan restaurants exist, and many places can adapt, but ask staff about ingredients and check the venue's own menu.

faqs.question: Which markets can I visit besides the Great Market Hall?
faqs.answer: Local-food writers and market sources mention the Rákóczi tér Market Hall in District VIII, the Lehel Market Hall in District XIII and the Fény utca market near Széll Kálmán tér. Hours and traders change, so check current details before going.
